author: Koch, GerdSchütze, Frieda
title: The South Seas -- yesterday and today: cultural change among the Tongans and an attempt to interpret this development
section: B. Games of Adults and Children
ocms: 177 Acculturation and Culture Contact; 178 Sociocultural Trends; 524 Games; 526 Athletic Sports; 857 Childhood Activities
text: Today, children play among themselves, for the most part also in European fashion. Following the example of adults, the boys like to play cricket and tennis. In this they are, of course, not pretentious; when they play tennis, for example, a rope stretched between two palm trees serves as the “net” and with a simple wooden bat they knock an old tennis ball over it. Marbles bought at the storekeeper's are popular among smaller boys. Many boys have little kites stretched with packing paper; these the boys also make more simply by 271 inserting the midribs of two coconut leaflets crosswise through a piece of paper torn from their school notebooks and then, with the help of a string, they let this simple wind-bird provided with a tapa tail climb five to fifteen meters into the air. Empty corned-beef cans with their colorful labels also serve as toys; boys aged about eight to twelve like to push around “can scooters” consisting of two such (low) cans forming “wheels” that are nailed to the ends of a short piece of wood in the center of which the “shaft” is fastened at right angles. Ten- to twelve-year-old boys often put together small sailboats with a halved coconut (or a wooden) hull and a tree leaf (or scrap of cotton) as a sail; they let this little boat sail in shallow water. Some boys also play with carved wooden propellers that are nailed to a small rod and that turn in the wind. Boys aged about eight to thirteen like to ride the 271 cont. surf—as did the men in ancient Tonga; several of them (up to about 20) let rather big waves carry them to the beach on box lids or other pieces of wood (approximately 70-100 centimeters long) which they use as “surfboards.” It is possible that the “pop-cork” game which the boys nowadays seldom play is of ancient Tongan origin.
note: Many boys have little kites covered with packing paper, or make simpler ones from two crossed coconut-leaflet midribs pushed through notebook paper, with a tapa tail, flown five to fifteen metres high.

author: Kaeppler, Adrienne Lois
title: Rank in Tonga
ocms: 554 Status, Role, and Prestige; 565 Classes; 581 Basis of Marriage; 582 Regulation of Marriage; 612 Kindreds and Ramages; 613 Lineages; 643 Chief Executive
text: A Tu'i Kanokupolu's son had lower kāinga status than his sister. The social repercussions that might result in suceeding generations could be prevented by cross-cousin marriage (or by marrying a foreigner, as in the Tu'i Tonga line). An example of such a cross-cousin marriage can be found in the ancestors of the present king (Figure 5). 25 25. Cross-cousin marriage ( kite tama ) was not prescribed, proscribed, or preferred, but was occasionally practiced among the highest chiefs to prevent social repercussions that might result if a Tu'i were outranked by a collateral line. The traditional incest rules seem to have been that one could marry his third cousin ( mokopuna tolu ), and cross-cousin marriage was not a perceived alternate in choosing a mate. Rather, cross-cousin marriage was a function of rank and a political move to prevent the interference of kāinga status principles at the societal level, and to assure that the offspring would have the highest possible rank within a certain line. This was a strategic Figure 4: Ha'a Affiliation of Tongan Noble Titles move because the descendants of Tevita 'Unga could be outranked by the descendants of his sister Sālote if married to someone of a higher ranking ha'a. By the marriage of the children of Tevita and Sālote no one within the Tu'i Kanokupolu line could outrank the offspring of this union. Tupou II married Lavinia of the Tu'i Tonga line, and their daughter, Sālote, who became Tupou III, thus combined the Tu'i Tonga and Tu'i Kanokupolu lines. Tupou III married the highest chief of Ha'a Takalaua, so that Tupou IV combines all three important lines. Tupou IV has married Mata'aho, who descends through her mother from the Tu'i Tonga line, and their children are now the ranking individuals of all of the three main ha'a.
note: Tongan kite tama "cross-cousin marriage".

author: Wilkinson, R. J. (Richard James), 1867-1941
title: Life and customs: Malay amusements
doc_page: 2Series: Papers on Malay subjects (The Government of the Federated States of Malaya)
text: In these quaint tags of old folklore we find one reason that endears the play of children to the anthropologist; in the wide range of some toys and games we get a second reason. When the members of the “Haddon” expedition visited Borneo they found that the local Dyaks could beat them easily at the game of cat's-cradle. Personally we fail to see what precise ethnological inference is to be deduced from the dire result of this international match; failure in such a contest must be admitted to cast a serious reflection on European prowess in infantile arts, but this may be due to the European habit of putting away childish things on the attainment of manhood. At all events, we may take it for granted that the game of cat's-cradle is widespread. So, too, is the use of the bull-roarer, a weird instrument, the noise of which is used by Papuan magicians to warn women away from their initiation ceremonies. The bull-roarer has been found in the Malay Peninsula in the form of a toy. But here again inference is dangerous. The wide range of tops and kites and the diffusion of a relatively modern game like chess should put us on our guard against rash ethnological conclusions. Then there is the pellet-bow. The pellet-bow is used as a weapon in Further India and only as a toy in Malaya. Is it in this country a discarded local weapon or an imported foreign toy? We cannot say. Conversely, the blowpipe, which is a weapon in Malaya, is only a toy in Nias. Must we conclude that the blowpipe ousted the bow in Sumatra while the bow ousted the blowpipe in Nias? It may be so; still, we cannot speak positively. The most unfortunate feature about this branch of anthropological research is that it supplies us with no solutions to the riddles in which it is so rich. Though a happy huntingground for the theorist, it is a bewildering labyrinth for a student of cautious temperament.
note: Author's general remark on the wide distribution of tops and kites as a caution against diffusion arguments.

author: Thomson, Joseph, 1858-1895

ocms: 237 Animal by-Products; 302 Personal Grooming; 714 Uniform and Accouterment; 726 Warfare
text: Let us pause and in imagination watch some enthusiastic young ditto buckling on the armour of her knight. First there is tied round his neck, whence it falls in flowing lengths, the nǎiberé, --a piece of cotton, six feet long, two feet broad, with a longitudinal stripe of coloured cloth sewed down the middle of it. Over his shoulders is placed a huge cape of kite's feathers--a regular heap of them. The kid-skin garment which hangs at his shoulder is now folded up, and tied tightly round his waist like a belt, so as to leave his arms free. His hair is tied into two pigtails, one before and one behind. On his head is placed a remarkable object formed of ostrich feathers stuck in a band of leather, the whole forming an elliptically-shaped head-gear. This is placed diagonally in a line beginning under the lower lip and running in front of the ear to the crown. His legs are ornamented with flowing hair of the colobus, resembling wings. His bodily adornment is finished off by the customary plastering of oil. His simè or sword is now attached--it does not hang--to his right side; and through the belt is pushed the skull-smasher or knobkerry, which may be thrown at an approaching enemy, or may give the quietus to a disabled one. His huge shield in his left hand and his great spear in his right complete his extraordinary equipment. For the rest you must imagine an Apollo-like form and the face of a fiend, and you have before you the beauideal of a Masai warrior. He takes enormous pride in his weapons, and would part with everything he has rather than his spear. He glories in his scars, as the true laurel and decorative marks of one who delights in battles.
note: Warrior's cape of kite feathers; the bird.

author: Sieroszewski, Wacław, 1858-1945
title: The Yakut: an experiment in ethnographic research

text: 646 When the shaman, assured of the protection of his amagyat', set out on the journey, then a cow was led out of the yurt into the yard and tied to a post prepared in advance, about one sagene high and with carvings on top, supposed to resemble the ordinary sarga (hitching-post). In front of this post were put up three smooth, planed posts of about the same size, with wooden figures of birds on top: first the two-headed winged dummy called eksekyu (fig. 160), then a sculpture of the same size of a kuagas, loon (fig. 157) or a raven, suor, and third, a smaller image of a cuckoo, kaga (fig. 156). The birds stand rather close to one another, one behind the other with their heads turned to the south. On the same line in front of them are placed nine green firs at a distance of a sagene from each other; their bark has been peeled off to a height of one sagene and more. Between the firs is stretched a thin rope of hair, decorated with tufts of white horse's hair. Starting from the first bird it rises higher and higher and is supposed to represent the road on which the shaman must fly to the heavens following the birds, driving before him the sacrificial cattle (fig. 155). (Namsk Ulus, 1889). In the grooves and secluded forest regions where various objects used only during shamanistic ceremonies are brought and left I sometimes observed, besides the birds, posts, firs, wooden figures, and hair ropes decorated with pieces of cloth and tufts of hair, seti, a sort of stand, about 647 one sagene high with nine small wooden goblets on the top cross-piece (fig. 161), bearing obvious traces of the blood which had recently filled them, and also small tables on high legs with pieces of meat, fat, and liver. In certain ceremonies they employ images of gulls, quail, grouse, and kites.
note: Images of kites, the birds, used in shamanic ceremonies.

author: Hamel, Hendrik
title: The description of the kingdom of Corea
doc_page: 130-131Journal: Transactions of the Korea Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society - Vol. 9
text: “By reason of this excessive Cold those who live on the Northern Coast feed only upon Barley, and that none of the best; for no Rice or Cotton can grow there. Those that are best to pass there have their Meal brought from the South. The poorer sort there have no Cloaths but what are made of Hemp and pitiful Skins. But to make amends the Root Nisy grows there, which they give to the Tartar [ER: the Mongols] for their Tribute, and drive a great Trade with it to China and Japan. The rest of the Country is fruitful, and produces all things necessary to support Life especially Rice, and other sorts of Grain. They have Hemp, Cotton and Silkworms; but they know not how to work the Silk. There is also Silver, Lead, Tyger's Skins, and the Nisy root, not to speak of Beasts and Fowl, and several other things. They have store of Horses and Cows, and make use of Oxen to till the Land, and Horses to travel, and carry goods from place to place. There are also Bears, Deer, Wild Bores, Swine, Dogs, Cats, and several other Creatures. We never saw any 131 Elephants's there, but Alligators or Crocodils of several Sizes, which keep in the Rivers. Their Back is Musket proof, but the skin of their Belly is very soft. Some of them are 18 or 20 Ells long, their Head large, the Snout like a Hog, the Mouth and Throat from Ear to Ear, the Eye sharp but very small, the teeth white and strong, plac'd like the teeth of a Comb. When they eat they only move the Upper Jaw. Their Backbone has 60 Joints, on their Feet are long Claws or Talons, their Tail is as long as the Body; they eat either Fish or Flesh, and are great lovers of Man's Flesh. The Coresians often told us, that three Children were once found in the Belly of one of these Crocodils. Besides these, there are abundance of Serpents and venomous Creatures. As for Fowl, they have Swans, Geese, Ducks, Herons, Storkes, Eagles, Faulcons, Kites, Pigeons, Woodcocks, Magpies, Daws, Larks, Lapwings, Pheasants, Hens, and plenty of them all as well as other sorts, not known in Europe. ”
note: Kites the birds in a list of Korean fowl.

text: As many members of the old head-hunting guilds are still alive it may be of interest to describe the special ritual formerly (and I believe still occasionally) followed on the death of one of these. The rites were carried out by the son, provided he himself belonged to the guild; otherwise by the head of the guild. The officiant (son, or principal head-getter) stood before the symbol (an abosse tree) and spoke as follows: ‘My father, I have brought to you this day a dog and chicken in order that I may be permitted to cut down your Obasi. When you are reborn slay not your own children, and may they not slay you. May you kill none by accident, but may you kill your enemies with the intent to do so. Whatever good you desire may it be accomplished.’ The dog and fowl were then killed, and the blood was allowed to flow on to the ground in front of the symbol. The symbol was then cut down and thrown into the ‘bush of evil’. The flesh of the dog and fowl was cooked and eaten by the warriors, young and old. During the feast old war-songs were sung, such as: ‘I am a kite which kills and carries off’, ‘I am an evil spirit ( Ekweesu ) for an unfortunate man’, ‘I am the killer of a woman's husband, and the woman mourned her loss in the compound’. In some communities the head-getter's emblem was an obo tree and was known as his ikenga (i.e. upper arm). Before it was cut down the prayer was: ‘When you are reborn may your ikenga stand straight. May you be a killer of enemies, and not of fellow clansmen. May your son, who is succeeding you, look after his family as you did.’ The officiant then took a matchet, and with a single blow struck off the head of the sacrificial ram. The symbol was now cut down and a feast held, the meat being dipped in a sauce of oil and pepper which had first been deposited in a human skull.
note: War song "I am a kite which kills and carries off"; the bird.

author: Maiskii, I. M. (Ivan Mikhailovich), 1884-1975Dayton, Mrs.Kunitz, Joshua
title: Contemporary Mongolia
text: The Animal Kingdom of Autonomous Mongolia, too, is not distinguished by any particular species. Among the domestic animals we find camels, horses, cattle, sheep, goats, pigs (the latter are kept only by the Chinese), dogs, cats. The wild animals and beasts deserving of mention are: the brown bear (found in the vicinity of lake Kosogol), the red wolf (found in abundance everywhere), the wild ass, in Mongolian — “khulan” (found in Western Mongolia), the wild boar (found on the river Tes, and also in Khangai, roe deer or maral (found in the forests of Khangai and Tannu-Ola), the badger, fox, wolverine, lynx, wild cat, sable, ermine, squirrel, marmot (in Mongolian “tarbagan”), and several kinds of antelope (especially the antelope “dzeren”). Marmots are found in great numbers in high, dry places, and the antelopes roam in the mountains and valleys, sometimes in vast herds. Our expedition more than once stampeded herds of “dzeren” of 200, 300, 400 and more heads. Among the birds in Autonomous Mongolia 12 are found: eagle, kites (in huge numbers), swans, geese, ducks, cranes, bustards, pheasants, crows, jackdaws, magpies (noted for extreme boldness: they peck the backs of horses and camels until they draw blood), eagle-owls, owls, woodpeckers, larks, titmice, sparrows, red bullfinches, blackbirds, guineahens, quail, snipe, and many others. The number of different birds found here up to the present time reaches 291. * * G. E. Grum-Grzhimailo, ibid., p. 522. Among the reptiles we find a comparatively small number of snakes (chiefly adders) — during our whole trip I saw them only three times — lizards, salamanders, etc. Lastly, from among the fishes in the Mongol rivers there are found: salmo trutta L., salmo fluviatilis Pall, grayling, perch pike, roach, osman, and some others. As the Mongols do not eat fish, the abundance of fish in many places is truly fabulous.
note: Kites the birds, abundant in Mongolia.

author: Hulbert, Homer B.
title: The passing of Korea
text: “The vegetable life of Korea is like that of other parts of the temperate zone, but there is a striking preponderance of a certain kind of pine, the most graceful of its tribe. It forms a conspicuous element in every scene. The founder of the dynasty preceding the present one called his capital Song-do, or Pine Tree Capital. It is a constant theme in Korean art, and plays an important part in legend and folk-lore in general. Being an evergreen, it symbolises eternal existence. There are ten things which Koreans call the chang sang pul sa , or ‘long-lived and deathless.’ They are the pine-tree, tortoise, rock, stag, cloud, sun, moon, stork, water and a certain moss of lichen named ‘the ageless plant.’ Pine is practically the only wood used in building either houses, boats, bridges or any other [13] structure. In poetry and imaginative prose it corresponds to the oak of Western literature. Next in importance is the bamboo, which though growing only in the southern provinces, is used throughout the land and in almost every conceivable way. The domestic life of the Korean would be thrown into dire confusion were the bamboo to disappear. Hats are commonly made of it, and it enters largely, if not exclusively, into the construction of fans, screens, pens, pipes, tub-hoops, flutes, lanterns, kites, bows and a hundred other articles of daily use. Take the bamboo out of Korean pictorial art and half the pictures in the land would be ruined. From its shape it is the symbol of grace, and from its straightness and the regular occurrence of its nodes it is the symbol of faithfulness. The willow is one of the most conspicuous trees, for it usually grows in the vicinity of towns, where it has been planted by the hand of man. Thus it becomes the synonym of peace and contentment. The mighty row of willows near Pyeng-yang in the north is believed to have been planted by the great sage and coloniser Kija in 1122 B. C., his purpose being to influence the semi-savage people by this object-lesson. From that time to this Pyeng-yang has been known in song and story as ‘The Willow Capital.’”
note: Bamboo enters into the construction of kites, among fans, lanterns, bows and other articles of daily use.

author: Dautcher, Jay, 1963-
title: Down a narrow road: identity and masculinity in a Uyghur community in Xinjiang China
ocms: 121 Theoretical Orientation; 186 Cultural Identity and Pride; 562 Gender Status; 855 Child Care; 857 Childhood Activities; 867 Transmission of Cultural Norms; 868 Transmission of Skills
text: The first part of the argument emerges in Chapters 4–6, which focus on the gendering processes of child rearing, childhood play activities, and adult gender relations, and which emphasize the position of boys and men in those activities. At infancy, as we saw in Chapter 4, all children have walnuts smeared on their mouths at birth in the hope that this will improve their ability to speak “crackingly.” This metaphor of “crackingness,” I have suggested, is best understood in the context of the verbal dueling so prominent in adult interactions, in particular as a metaphor for the capacity of the dominant individual to “crack” a cognitive frame offered by an opponent through a witty or aggressively assertive remark. Male infants are further made aware of their gendered sociality in infancy through the playful interactions of adult female kin, who symbolically consume boys’ genitals, reinforcing for boys their need to continually demonstrate their masculinity through personal display. The language of endearment used for boys one to four years old is explicitly recognized as a potentially feminizing influence that boys must be sure to reject as they grow out of early childhood. When boys mature to the ages of four to seven, older men taunt them by pulling down their pants, asking them if they are boys or girls, continuing this process of gender identity enculturation. In the semi-autonomous play activities that preoccupy boys during the years from seven to puberty (these include kite flying, top spinning, and hoop rolling), older boys continue to express a concern with keeping themselves or their symbolic extensions in erect postures, a trait that continues to be used as a key metaphor of domination throughout adult life. Also in their play activities, boys begin to express a concern with performing dominance in front of audiences of other boys. In adult gender relations, these same concerns are repeatedly expressed in men's attitudes toward sexual relations with women, as revealed in narratives that convey men's anxieties regarding their ability to dominate women and to render women's sexuality subordinate to their own.
note: Kite flying, top spinning and hoop rolling are semi-autonomous play activities of boys from seven to puberty, read as displays of erectness and dominance.

author: Sciorra, Joseph
title: 'We're not here just to plant. We have culture.': an ethnography of the South Bronx Casita Rincón Criollo

text: A visit to Rincón Criollo is enough to dispel the erroneous notion that traditional Puerto Rican culture is “weak” in the material arts. 15 15 Nathan Glazer and Daniel Patrick Moynihan's uninformed observations of Puerto Rican material culture and their racist conclusions are found in the book, Beyond the Melting Pot: The Negroes, Puerto Ricans, Jews, Italians, and the Irish of New York City (Cambridge, Massachusetts: M.I.T. Press, 1968), p. 88. Rincón Criollo serves as a workshop where various types of hand drums are repaired and crafted. The late Franciso “Paco” Rivera once fashioned bomba drums from recycled pickle and salt cod barrels at the site and in his nearby storefront workshop. Miguel “Micky” Sierra of Arecibo apprenticed himself to Paco to deepen his knowledge of drum craftsmanship at the casita. Panderetas (hand-held frame drums used in playing plena) are the principal musical instruments produced at the casita from discarded cooking pots and goat skins imported from Puerto Rico. In addition, Chema designs and makes his own kites and Paco carved miniature portraits of black men and women from the seeds of the corroso plant as jewelry charms at Rincón Criollo. Composer and artisan Benny Ayala uses the casita to turn newspaper, flour, and paint into the polychromatic, multi-horned masks of the vejigante, a costumed demon who torments children and adults during carnival festivities in Ponce. As Chema pointed out, “ No estamos aquí sólo para sembrar. Nosotros tenemos cultura. ” [We're not here just to plant. We have culture.] 16 16 Conversation with José Manuel “Chema” Soto, 17 June 1988. Paco's musical instruments and Benny's vejigante masks were featured in the 1988–89 El Museo del Barrio exhibition, “¡Folklore!: Traditional Crafts from Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico made in New York.”
note: A man at the Rincón Criollo casita in the South Bronx designs and makes his own kites, among other traditional crafts made there.

author: Kroeber, A. L. (Alfred Louis), 1876-1960
title: The Arapaho
ocms: 171 Comparative Evidence; 531 Decorative Art; 534 Musical Instruments; 561 Age Stratification; 575 Sodalities; 756 Shamans and Psychotherapists; 796 Organized Ceremonial
text: Rawhide rattles of a shape typical on the Plains—consisting of a spherical or somewhat elongated head two or three inches in diameter, and a straight handle about six inches long—occur among the Arapaho. Rattles of this character seem to be used by the seven old men constituting the highest society in the ceremonial organization. On the whole, however, the use of rattles of this type is characteristic of the medicine-man and his individual supernatural powers, and not of the tribal ceremonies. In most of these ceremonies, rattles are either not used, as in the crazy-dance, or consist of bunches of hoofs attached to sticks, as in the dog-dance. Rawhide rattles are used in the star-dance, the first preliminary to the series of tribal ceremonies; but these rattles are small, kite-shaped, and flat, thus differing very distinctly from the globular or oval, or even sausage-shaped rattles, of the medicine-men. Among the Gros Ventre the same distinction exists between the star-dance rattle and the ordinary medicine-man's rattle, Fig. 178 was originally published in this location though the Gros Ventre star-dance rattle is quite different from that of the Arapaho. The medicine-men's rattles under present consideration are made of two pieces of hide firmly sewed together, the stitched seam passing up one side of the handle and the head, over the top of the head, and down the other side. The head is apparently sewed when the hide is green, and dried over a filling of sand. The rattling is said to be produced by gravel. A stick is inserted in the handle, and the handle is almost always wrapped with cloth, skin, or thongs. Usually, feathers or similar ornaments are attached to thongs at the very top of the rattle; and in many cases cloth, skin, or other hanging substances fall from the lower end of the handle. Most of the globular rattles are streaked with vertical lines or incisions. It is not clear how these are produced. In some specimens they are sufficiently marked to cause the head of the rattle to have a distinctly corrugated appearance. In one case they would seem to have been burnt in.

As an afterthought Fernoch reads El Vate's elegy to his poet-friend Lorenzo, who has died in his arms in the desert. The elegy buries not only his friend but El Vate himself: Alive “he wished to make the desert flower with poems. Ecstatically, he went forth to plant metaphlowers and fountains with jests of polychrome letters, his red blood, lakes, jungles, and the vivid irises of his fantasy.” 59 59. Ibid., 138. Their “public” and “personal” selves thus become extinguished by a society that quickly discards the former and disregards the latter. 61 61. The water trickling down from the mask did not therefore enter his mouth and therefore he did not die. All the other men died as ukpe, which was really poison but used for painting the mask, got wet and entered their mouths. author: Evans-Pritchard, E. E. (Edward Evan), 1902-1973
title: Nuer marriage ceremonies
text: On the following morning take place three rites which may on no account be omitted, the sacrifice (which may take place the evening before), the lustration, and the shaving of the bride's head. The sacrificial beast should be an ox, but if the bridegroom's father is poor, and at this stage of the marriage he is likely to be hard up, the yang muot, the ‘cow’ of the consummation, may be a goat, or even just beer. The bridegroom's gu an buthui rubs ashes on its back, calls out the spear-name of his lineage and speaks of the beast and the bride, telling the spirits and ghosts of his lineage to witness the union and to bless it with sons so that the lineage may continue. He says to them, ‘Now you see your ox; you see this maid; let her be a good wife; let her bear many children, many sons; let her work well in her husband's home, milk the cows, dry the cattle dung; let her be a faithful wife and not a profligate’; and so forth, asking them to make the union a lasting and happy one. He then spears the ox and it is cut up by the wife's people, the visitors, and divided among them in the customary portions, only the head, neck, and a few other pieces of meat going to the people of the bridegroom. The visiting maidens at once cook and eat the ribs, kidneys, and stomach, besides filling themselves with porridge and beer, the bride alone abstaining because she may not eat in the home of her mother-in-law. They take the rest of the carcass back to their homes for their elders. As generally happens when there is a feast, outsiders, persons not of the bridegroom's closest kin, hang about the carcass like kites when it is being cut up, hoping to obtain a piece of meat by begging, snatching, or persistently getting in the way. There is much shouting, argument, and general confusion. The gwan buthni may perform another duty associated with his office in anointing the bride with butter. Her father will already have blessed her in this manner before she set out to go to her husband's home.
note: Ethnographer's simile: people hang about a carcass like kites.

author: Collocott, E. E. V. (Ernest Edgar Vyvyan), 1886-
title: The supernatural in Tonga
ocms: 787 Revelation and Divination; 791 Magicians and Diviners; 793 Priesthood
text: The fact that supernatural forces and beings manifest themselves through material agencies would invest with importance the office of those who were skilled in reading the signs. One Tongan stated that those who had no god to apply to had recourse to a diviner ( tongafiji ), adding the interesting detail that there was aruspication by examination of the blood of animals. Another said that he thought that each god had his own diviner, but the most trustworthy statements show no evidence of a class of diviners attached to the gods apart from the priests. A certain cowrie shell god used to give indications of his will by movements, as by standing up on end. War clubs, presumably those kept in the temples, were consulted on the expediency of going to war. If the club shook that was the god giving his vote for war, but if it remained still that was a declaration against the opening of hostilities. Whilst, however, the interpretation of the will of the gods was the function of the priests, there were diviners ( tongafiji ) who, without being priests or being attached in any special way to a particular god, were able to see what was distant in time and space. The word kikite which is used of divination and foretelling seems to contain the same root as the word kite which is used of the appearance of anything at a distance, particularly of land showing up when one is out at sea. I have not been able to discover that these diviners were reputed to be inspired by any god, but they seem merely to have seen and declared things by some inward light of their own. A rather circumstantial account is preserved of a famous soothsayer named Hema who knew from the island of Eua the progress of a single-sticks match in Tongatabu in which a local champion was opposed by a mighty fighter from Eua. Hema kept the Eua people posted on the progress of the contest with the promptness and certainty of a wireless installation and had the melancholy duty of informing them of the defeat of their own champion. His best remembered exploit was that of telling a chief the time at which a pet bird, which had flown away and was many days overdue, would return. Not content with the bald statement as to the day and time at which the chief would again see his bird he gave a detailed itinerary of the homeward flight.
note: Tongan kite "appearance of something at a distance".

author: Jones, Philip
title: Namatjira: traveller between two worlds
doc_page: 131Journal: The Heritage of Namatjira : the watercolourists of central Australia, edited by Jane Hardy, J. V. S. Megaw, and M. Ruth Megaw
ocms: 177 Acculturation and Culture Contact; 532 Representative Art; 546 Motion Picture Industry; 579 Brawls, Riots, and Banditry; 778 Sacred Objects and Places
text: Within the structured confines of Hermannsburg society, Namatjira was apparently on safe ground in his artistic allusions to restricted subjects. This was so at least until after the Second World War, by which time the Mission had become less isolated from other communities in Central Australia. 82 In 1949 Mountford's documentary film on Namatjira was shown at Hermannsburg to Haast Bluff people. Strehlow recorded the fact that chaos broke out among the audience when a segment documenting (presumably) sacred rock art was shown. Women and children ran from the room and trouble was expected from Haast Bluff men as a result. This was later resolved, but it can be assumed that Namatjira himself would have received much of the blame for this transgression (Strehlow Journals, Book 14, 2 October 1949). In the meantime, Aranda artists, led by Namatjira, were able to develop a style in which even human and animal figures, let alone events, ceremonies or sacred objects, seem superfluous. A Pitjantjatjara ceremony, a crucifixion scene complete with Roman legionnaires (see Fig. 1.16), or a watercolour in which three sacred objects hang in the air like massive Zeppelins (Fig. 3.23), each confronted the viewer with a worrying incongruity. There is a dissonance in these works between apparently discrete and definite subjects and apparently timeless landscapes. In fact, none of the subjects can be fixed in time. To the Aranda artists working during the 1930s and 1940s, and even later, the crucifixion, the ceremony, the sacred objects and even apparently mundane hunting scenes have existed, like the Dreaming itself, within another power-filled dimension of present reality. 83 The same may well be true of apparently mundane hunting scenes which are represented with remarkable consistency by Aranda artists, from Jimmy Kite through the Namatjira sketches and early watercolours, the work of Enos Namatjira to the recent painting of Marie Abbott. This consistency of expression indicates that these artists are not simply describing a scene which they have observed, but are reiterating an entrenched aspect of their culture and history. And the landscape in these paintings, while remaining Aranda in essence, has been rendered as European and so contains Western notions of space and time. The dissonance between a precise event and a timeless landscape can also be seen as its opposite: a finite view which frames a transcending event.
note: Jimmy Kite, an Aranda artist.

text: Now, after creating these creatures, Itbu-moo called them near her to receive the final gifts before they went out into this wide world to manage on their own. She told them that, before they approached her, consulting over their different needs and requirements with the other creatures, they should form themselves into groups with those who had similar views and requirements, and then come together to her in an orderly fashion. First arrived the group which came and said that since they would be all on their own, they would ask for a gift with which they could protect themselves from the others. This group included buffaloes, bulls, cows, deer, stags, and similar creatures; they took away horns with them. After they had left came those who said they would appreciate fighting and scrapping because, without fighting and scrapping, they would get nowhere. Hearing this, and looking at this group, Itmu-moo gave a wry smile and said, “Be it so.” Led by the lion, tiger, leopard and others, they took away sharp claws and fangs with them. Now, when Itbu-moo was busy distributing gifts to the rather unruly groups, she could see from the corner of her eyes one particular creature, the human being, who was standing on one side, not trying to force his way in, but giving a sporting chance to others; and standing by demurely. Next came the party which thought that the eartheings would be too troublesome to allow them to make a good living. So, they asked for a gift that would free them from this predicament. Appreciating this demand, Itbu-moo smiled a little and said, “You are blessed with powerful wings to float and fly in the sky.” The vulture, kite, crow and other birds instantly took to their wings and left the place. Then came the turn of another group of creatures who said that, since the land and the sky were overcrowded, they would be happy to occupy the seas, rivers, and oceans; and they would like this gift. Itbu-mu said, “You shall have special lungs, fins, tails and some of you will have coats of fur.” Straightaway they dived into the water, and started sporting around in a blissful manner. One big group thus came to occupy one of Itbu-moo's major creations, the seas.

title: A note on the Masai system of relationship
section: A NOTE ON THE MASAI SYSTEM OF RELATIONSHIP AND OTHER MATTERS CONNECTED THEREWITH.

text: When listening to Masai talking to one another it would often appear as if many of the terms of relationship used were the same as names of cattle, sheep, goats, and donkeys, etc. This is chiefly due to the fact that whenever a woman is brought into the family by marriage it is customary for her husband's relations and their wives to give her an animal to show that she is recognized as a member of the family. The giver and the recipient ever afterwards call one another after the animal which has been given, to which the particle pa- is prefixed. Thus, a man gives his brother's wife or his paternal uncle's wife, or his paternal uncle's son's wife a cow, a calf, or a lamb, and the terms of address used by the two, instead of being par-sidan or yeiyo, as the case may be, are pa-kite[unknown] ng, pa-ashe, or pa-supen; a father-in-law gives his daughter-in-law a calf, and the two call one another pa-ashe; and a paternal uncle gives his nephew's wife a she-goat and calls her pa-kine. Similarly a man's first wife usually presents each successive wife with a calf on her marriage, and instead of using the term na-aïni when speaking to one another the two women say pa-ashe; a woman gives her husband's brother's wife a donkey as a wedding present, and the two women call one another pa-sighiria; and a mother-in-law selects a cow for her daughter-in-law some months after marriage, when she has learnt to keep house for her husband, and the form of address is pa-kitc[unknown] ng. This method of address is carried even further, and is used between men of the same family. A father, for instance, usually gives his son a bull when the boy is eight or nine years of age, and the two call one another pa-oi[unknown] ng[unknown] oni instead of papa and li-ay[unknown] oni; a paternal uncle makes a similar present to his nephew, and the same form of address is used; an elder brother gives his younger brother a heifer, and the two call one another pa-'n-danwo; and paternal cousins often use the terms pa-oro or pa-meregesh when talking to each other.
note: Maasai pa-kiteng, a term of address from a gift animal.

author: Cushing, Frank Hamilton, 1857-1900
title: Zuñi breadstuff
section: CHAPTER XIX CORN DANCES AND FESTIVALS
text: On a certain summer evening of the fourth, or, as the case may be, eighth year, a curious figure—a veritable ideal chimney-sweep—appears. Black as the soot with which he is painted can make him, is he; bristling at many points with tufts of hair and cedar brushes. His head is round like FIG. 14.—Demon inspector of ovens an oven; round too his eyes, like flue-holes, with yellow ladders painted over them for brows. A bunch of stiff hair surmounts his crown, out of which issues, like a flame, a red eagle-plume to symbolize fire. His mouth is almost square, like an oven-door, but with red lips—the light gleaming out when the stone door is closed—with a stiff, thin beard shooting forth from its under side which makes it look, despite its parallelogrammic proportions, like a cyclopean eye with heavy winkers, placed too low down. On either cheek is painted, in glaring yellow, the paw of a badger or some other famous burrower—also symbolic of function. The creature carries in one hand a wand of yucca leaves with which to scourge away dogs, and in the other a little broom of hemlock. To his rump is fastened a long cord of fiber, like the tail of a kite. As he travels along, he staggers, crooks his thighs, crawls eccentrically from side to side, and plunges this way and that as though seeking for or trying to enter ovens; for in everything he sees nothing but ovens—sometimes mistakes ladders or even burros for such and strives to get into them. When at last he espies a veritable oven, he leaps wildly toward it with a low growl of satisfaction, and eagerly disappears through its dark doorway. Presently out come crumbs and fragments of bread or bits of he'-we (left there, of course, in anticipation of his visit), which scarcely strike the ground before they are grabbed up by the ever attendant Kâ'-ye-mä-shi, or Ne'-we. Dust and cinders follow—as though the oven had never been cleaned!—nor do the exertions of the Oven Demons cease short of mischief to the masonry of the structure, unless one of his companions, with great to-do, snakes him forth by means of the long rope of fiber. No sooner is he out, than he turns on his captor with his yucca weapon and breaks away, and goes plunging along to another oven, and so on until every dome-shaped bread receptacle in the village has been duly visited and purified.
note: Ethnographer's simile: a cord fastened to a dancer's rump like the tail of a kite.

author: Raybeck, Douglas
title: Mad dogs, Englishmen, and the errant anthropologist: fieldwork in Malaysia

text: Lately an increase in the influence of Islamic fundamentalism has led to some assaults on traditional Kelantanese culture. Within the last year, such traditional entertainment forms as the shadow play (wayang kulit), top spinning, and kite flying have either been banned or inhibited. Traditional curing ceremonies ( main puteri ) and mak yong, a form of opera indigenous to the area, have also just been banned. There are also a series of efforts to curtail the freedom of women. Those women with whom I have spoken recently are not pleased with these attempts. An excerpt from field notes of two years ago: We talked longer about religion, and she clarified her views on Islam and current changes in its practice. She is quite annoyed with dakwah [the fundamentalist movement] and their posturings. She mentioned that there are those who think they are better than others because they are dakwah, yet many of them are comparatively ignorant of religious matters. She said they are unfamiliar with hukum [used here to mean religious law]. She also noted that there were some who didn't even pray regularly though they continue to posture. And from a male during the same research: He seemed displeased with some aspects of the Islamic resurgence that has occurred over the past years. He notes that now, people who wear uniforms can alter those in order to add religious elements. He clearly did not approve of this development. He added that people who objected to such headgear changes were accused of being against Islam. He stated that the interpretation for acceptable behavior had become more narrow and less tolerant. The power of the fundamentalists in Kelantan is not unlike that of some in our own society who claim special access to the moral high ground. To oppose such individuals is to oppose morality, or in the case of the Kelantanese, Islam. I am perturbed by these developments partly because they contravene some elements of Kelantanese culture that I have always thought admirable. Historically, Kelantanese have subscribed to what they sometimes term a broad path ( jalan lebar ) and, like the Javanese (Anderson 1965), have been accepting of a range of behaviors and beliefs, so long as these were not threatening to village interests. The Kelantanese, like other Malays and many Indonesians, subscribed to the concept “Other fields, other grasshoppers” (Lain padang, lain belalang). Only two years ago one older man, upset with the narrow and exclusive worldview promoted by dakwah members, expressed to me his conviction, “There is only one God, but there may be many roads to him.”
note: Kite flying, with shadow play and top spinning, is a traditional Kelantanese entertainment recently banned or inhibited under Islamic fundamentalist influence.

text: Then a bloody tumor grew on the leg of Lowa, from which, when it burst open, emerged Wulleb (1) 1. Wulleb. This word may come from wut, “jasmine-like tree,” and leb ( lab ), big, full-grown. On the other hand, however, there is no other case of a tenuis becoming a liquid through regressive assimilation. Therefore, it would appear that this word comes from wun or un (both words occur with the same meaning; cf. wunne, “upper thigh”): ground, reason, place where something grows or sits firmly. In this sense Wulleb would mean the bottom of the sea, on which the rock rests, or also the oldest created being. The same idea is in the name for Wulleb in the Ratak group, Iroej: i = always; roej = island reef left bare and dry by the receding water, thus, an atoll raised above sea level. This interpretation is confirmed by the fact that Wulleb and Lejman are both serpents / Würmer / in the Ratak tale and consequently analogous. Lejmān, however, means a loose stone lying on the reef. Thus, Wulleb was the lower serpent or the fixed island reef, whereas Lejmān, the upper serpent or loose rock, was lifted up by means of a bar in order to form the firmament. This also explains the natives' idea that the firmament is solid and can be walked upon. — Uellip is a misspelling. and Limdunānij (2) 2. Limdunānij might come from lim, “folded,” dun, “eel,” ānij, “spirit” (cf. lim-āk-āk, “folded like a frigate bird” — a paper kite) and refer to the circular shape of the atolls. Or it might be that the word is — as seems more probable to me — made up of lüm, “slimy secretion, slime, excrement,” du, “anus,” 'n (for in ), apposition particle, anij, “spirit” and signifies the rocky soil and the fertile ground. . 309 cont. Limdunanij gave birth to two male beings: Lanej (3) 3. Lanēj. La, “master,” an, “his,” ēj, “above, heights”: zenith. . (Master of the Heights), and Lewōj (4) 4. Lewōj. La, “master,” w, euphonic connecting sound, ōj, “middle of island”: nadir. (Master of the Middle of the Island). 309 cont. Wulleb and his sister's children sat down one day on the stalk of an arrowroot, which, growing up to the vault of the sky, enabled them to ascend. Their peaceful companionship, however, was of short duration. Soon the brothers plotted to kill their uncle, and the latter, exhausted by long night watches, finally fell from the vault of the sky.
note: In an etymological note, lim-āk-āk, "folded like a frigate bird", is given as the word for a paper kite.

author: Scott, James George, Sir, 1851-1935
title: The Burman: his life and notions
section: CHAPTER XI THE LADDER OF EXISTENCE
ocms: 000 Material Not Relevant; 772 Cosmology; 779 Theological Systems
text: NOTWITHSTANDING the change, the pain, and the vanity of everything upon earth, yet the Lu-pyi, the Manôt-tha-bông, the state of man, is desirable beyond all others. Transience, misery, unreality prevail in all the thirty-one seats of the world, even in the twenty superior heavens, where those acted on by Kāma, generating beings, find no entrance. The Déwas come down to our earth from their six seats of bliss; the Byammās, even to the fourth state of Zān, are occasionally found in earthly guise in the precincts of holy monasteries; even Yahandas, who have entered into Thodda, the current of perfection, and after death attain the dreamful joy of Ne'ban, the cessation from existence, even these immaterial beings diffuse a saintly presence over the Southern Island. The great Lord Gautama appeared in the seat of man and preached the sacred law, and he preached it there because all the twenty-seven Buddhas before him had done the same, and when he preached it on that soft Indian eve, I know it writ that they who heard Were more—lakhs more—crores more—than could be seen, For all the Devas and the Dead thronged there, Till Heaven was emptied to the seventh zone, And uttermost dark Hells opened their bars; Also the daylight lingered past its time In rose-leaf radiance on the watching peaks, So that it seemed Night listened in the glens And Noon upon the mountains; yea! they write, The Evening stood between them like some maid, Celestial, love-struck, rapt; the smooth-rolled clouds Her braided hair; the studded stars the pearls And diamonds of her coronal; the moon Her forehead jewel, and the deepening dark Her woven garments. 'Twas her close-held breath Which came in scented sighs across the lawns While our Lord taught, and, while he taught, who heard— Though he were stranger in the land, or slave, High caste or low, come of the Aryan blood, Or Mlech or Jungle-dweller, seemed to hear What tongue his fellows talked. Nay, outside those Who crowded by the river, great and small, The birds and beasts and creeping things—'tis writ— Had sense of Buddha's vast embracing love And took the promise of his piteous speech; So that their lives—prisoned in shape of ape, Tiger, or deer, shagged bear, jackal, or wolf, Foul-feeding kite, pearled dove, or peacock gemmed, Squat toad, or speckled serpent, lizard, bat; Yea, or of fish fanning the river-waves— Touched meekly at the skirts of brotherhood With man who hath less innocence than these; And in mute gladness knew their bondage broke Whilst Buddha spake these things before the King.
note: Foul-feeding kite, the bird, in a poem.

But after Liholiho's funeral and the institution of a Christian polity by the Ka'ahumanu mā, the issue of kingship was again associated with the Makahiki—and thus with a certain unruliness. By the same transformation that made the ruling woman Ka'ahumanu the keeper of the faith, Kauikeaouli (Kamehameha III) would be the prince of misrule. author: Beckwith, Martha Warren, 1871-1959Loumala, Katharine
title: Hawaiian mythology
text: (b) Fornander (1) and Rice version. Maihuna and Malai-a-ka-lani have five children in Hanamaulu on Kauai: Kawelo-mahamahaia, Kawelo-lei-ko`o, Kawelo-lei-makua (the subject of the story), and Kawelo-kamalama, all sons, and Kaena-ku-a-ka-lani, a daughter. The maternal grandparents bring up Kawelo at Wailua with Ai-kanaka (Man-eater), son of the ruling chief, and Kaua-hoa (Battle comrade), all relatives born on the same day. Kawelo eats enormously and angers his fellows by outdoing Kauahoa in managing toy boats and kite flying. The place where he worsted Kauahoa in the latter sport is called to this day Ka-ho`oleina-a-pe`a (The kite caused to fall). When the family move to Oahu, he angers his brothers by outdoing them in wrestling and they leave him and return to Kauai. Kawelo remains, becomes proficient in fishing, and fishes up the Uhumakaikai by means of a chant. When summoned to Kauai to avenge his family he sends his wife Kane-wahine-iki-aohe to obtain from her father the stroke called Wahieloa to prepare him for fighting. He bathes in the stream Apuakehau and gets a good meal of food. He sends Kamalama to spy upon the conversation of his wife's relatives and they believe him to be a god. At Waianae he builds a temple to his god Kane-i-ka-pualena and to the god Ka-lani-hehu which the messengers have brought him from Kauai. [...]
note: In the legend of Kawelo, the hero angers his fellows by outdoing Kauahoa at kite flying; the place where he beat him is still called Ka-ho`oleina-a-pe`a, "The kite caused to fall".

text: [...] They hire out their services to the village people who may need aid in the construction of a large house, and to the Bangkhuad and other community wats for building a new sala or repairing a deteriorating wat building. Two of them manufacture household implements, such as coconut scrapers, axe handles, wooden shovels, etc. One carpenter gains additional income by making chopsticks which he sells to the Chinese. Another specializes in making Siamese violins ( sau u and sau duang ). Mr. X has constructed two small boats ( ryabinthabad ). He sold one for 200 baht in 1951 and uses the other himself. Another carpenter was elected to be on the wat committee because of his knowledge of carpentry and the advice he could proffer concerning the large new sala to be constructed. Included in the six is one monk who makes coffins, kites, and mango pickers. Until a few years ago, the carpenters' main trade came from the construction of plows. The plows today are bought rough-hewn in Bangkok, and the carpenter merely finishes the rough edges. One carpenter's income can be broken down as follows: coconut scrapers — 10 to 15 baht; mango catchers — 10 baht; chopsticks — 25 baht per hundred; plow repair — 10 to 15 baht; services by the day — 30 baht; violins — 75 to 100 baht (only one violin was made in the past four years). His average yearly income from this trade is 900 baht. d) Two members of the community are reputed for their culinary talents. For weddings and large housewarmings, they are hired to help with the cooking, and for this they receive 10 baht plus food. [...]
note: Among the village carpenters is a monk who makes coffins, kites and mango pickers for income.

text: There is, however, in the collection of models of ships and boats at South Kensington, a small model which throws much light upon the practice in this region. This model, which was exhibited in the International Fisheries' Exhibition in London, and was sent by the Straits Settlements Commission, represents a couple of 'Malays fishing for gar-fish, Singapore'
note: A museum model shows Malays at Singapore fishing for garfish with rods and small palm-leaf kites trailing a shrimp-baited noose; Balfour suspects the method came with immigrants from Java.

locality: Tanara, north coast of Bantam, West Java; Thousand Isles
author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: From Java itself the fishing-kite is described by Dr P. N. van Kampen, who refers to its employment by fishermen of the village of Tanara on the north coast of Bantam, West Java, who extend their fishery into the Bay of Batavia.
note: Fishermen of Tanara (Bantam) and the Thousand Isles fish for garfish from anchored praus with a rod and a kite of epiphytic fern leaf, the tail replaced by a baited fibre noose; van Kampen suggests Buginese introduced it.

locality: Bawean Island, north of East Java
author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: The pamatpat landajang of Bawean Island is identical with the pantjing lajangan of Tanara.
note: Kite-fishing with rod and noose on Bawean Island, identical to the Javanese method.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: (The same leaf is used as a kite by children in Celebes.)
note: Children in Celebes fly kites of a fern leaf for pleasure; no particular people named.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: In the Banda Islands a rod is used having a ring at the upper end through which the line passes. The kite is made of a long, narrow leaf and from it hangs the lower part of the line which terminates either in a running-noose of copper wire upon which is threaded a small fish as bait, or in a fish-hook
note: Weber saw garfish caught in the Banda Islands with a rod-flown kite of a long narrow leaf trailing a baited copper-wire noose or a hook.
link_note: The Banda records describe kite fishing on Banda Neira between 1880 and 1913, after the Dutch conquest of 1621 had largely replaced the population; linked to Banda Malay, the language of the islands since then, rather than to Banda, which is now spoken in the Kei Islands. The older picture from Middleton's voyage of 1604-06, which Plischke lists first, is from Ternate (Anell 1955: 35-36).

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: In Gisser, an interesting modification in the apparatus is seen, which helps to link the fishing-kite of the Malayan Archipelago with that of Melanesia. Instead of a bait, a special kind of lure is employed, consisting of a tangle of spider's web attached to the extremity of the trailing line.
note: Kite-fishing for garfish on Geser with a spider-web lure instead of bait, the westernmost use of the cobweb lure.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: An excellent description of the Moluccan varieties of the fishing-kite is given by Max Weber, who saw this method of fishing for gar-fish practised in the Banda Islands, in Gisser (to the east of Ceram), in Ternate (west of Gilolo), and in Karakelang (Talauer Islands).
note: Weber saw kite-fishing for garfish practised on Ternate.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: In Karakelang, according to Weber (op. cit.), the rod is absent, the line being wound on a wooden spool held in the hand. The kite is made of a large dried leaf very like that used in West Java, but strengthened by the insertion of a pair of slender rods threaded through the leaf near the margins
note: On Karakelang the fishing kite of a large dried leaf stiffened with two slender rods is flown by hand from a canoe on a spool, trailing a hook about 20 metres from the kite.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: Dr C. G. Seligmann tells me that he was informed that the fishing-kite is employed on Normanby Island in the D'Entrecasteaux group.
note: Seligman was told that the fishing kite is used on Normanby Island (hearsay).

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: It is certainly used freely in Dobu, an island lying between Normanby Island and Ferguson Island, at the east end of Dawson Strait.
note: Dobu fishermen fly from small canoes a kite of four Morinda leaves sewn and stiffened with palm midribs, trailing a spider-web tassel that snags the garfish's teeth; the kite is called daune (or dauni).

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: Miss Beatrice Grimshaw has described the use of the fishing-kite on Kitava Island in the Trobriand group, though, unfortunately, she gives no figure of the apparatus. The kite is described as made of dried banana leaves stretched on twigs.
note: Grimshaw describes kite-fishing on Kitava with a kite of dried banana leaves on twigs and a spider-web lure, sometimes on a racquet-like frame.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: The practice of kite-fishing for gar-fish was seen by the Cooke-Daniels expedition in the Marshall Bennet Islands, lying east-south-east of the Trobriand group
note: Kite-fishing for garfish was seen in the Marshall Bennett Islands; Seligman's specimen is an oval kite of sewn palm-leaf strips with a spider-web lure.

text: Among some drawings made in 1895 for Lieut. B. T. Somerville, R.N., of H.M.S. Penguin, by a native of the Mungeri district of New Georgia, are two which represent fishing scenes
note: Drawings by a New Georgia man appear to show fishing from a canoe with a kite and a web lure; Balfour's inference, not a direct report.

author: Balfour, Henry
title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: In the eastern part of the Solomon group, including the large islands of Malaita and San Cristoval, this method of fishing is commonly practised.
note: On Malaita garfish are taken with a kite (rau) of sago-palm or ivory-nut leaf flown by a paddler who holds the line in his teeth, trailing a looped spider-web lure (after Guppy and Edge-Partington's salt-water people).

text: European travellers in China are amused to see grown-up people walking out in the evening, string in hand, leading their kites about like pet animals, and in some parts one day in the year (the 9th of the 9th month) has been given up from ancient times to a great kite-flying festival on the hills, when the sky is full of paper birds and monsters.
note: Grown men fly kites in the evening, and the ninth day of the ninth month is a kite-flying festival on the hills, with paper birds and monsters.

The native myth was that in the shades below, the god Tane once challenged the god Rongo to a game of kite-flying
note: Gill's Mangaian kites of reed with leaves and feathers on the tails, egg-, club- or bird-shaped, flown by old men on hilltops; in myth Rongo beat Tane at kite-flying, and the first kite up in each game is sacred to Rongo and bears his name.

author: Tylor, Edward B.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: The ordinary Chinese kites are made of a light, elastic framework of bamboo over which is spread a sheet of strong paper painted in brilliant hues with human or animal figures.
note: Chinese kites of bamboo and painted paper in many forms (dragons, centipedes up to forty feet, birds, insects, fish); men are expert fliers and boys have flown kites since the Song; Laufer credits China with inventing the kite, and Li Ye was a kite purveyor to the emperor.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: The ninth day of the ninth month in the autumn is devoted to the festival called Ch'ung-yang which is celebrated by ascending hills. Friends and acquaintances join for a picnic on some eminence in the neighborhood of their town and set kites adrift, as the autumnal breezes favor the sport. This also is the great day for holding kite contests.
note: At the Ch'ung-yang festival (ninth day of the ninth month) people picnic on hills and set kites adrift, and hold kite contests with cords stiffened with crushed glass or porcelain to cut rivals down.
link_note: EA Kiangsu used as a Han Chinese proxy.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: This music has a beneficial effect, for it is thought to scour evil spirits from the atmosphere.
note: Kites carry bamboo flutes or musical bows whose sound is thought to scour evil spirits from the air; captive kites are tied to roofs to hum through the night, and lanterns and fire-crackers are sent up the line.
link_note: EA Kiangsu used as a Han Chinese proxy.

text: Kites were originally used in China for military signalling and for such purposes only
note: Kites were first used for military signalling; traditions tell of Han Sin measuring distance with a kite and of besieged generals sending messages by kite in 549 and 781.

text: The idea that a kite functions as a scapegoat charming away the owner's sins and misfortunes is a recent development to be found locally and sporadically, but it is not general; it is more developed in Korea than in China
note: Kites as scapegoats carrying away the owner's sins and misfortunes are found locally in China.
link_note: EA Kiangsu used as a Han Chinese proxy.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: As in China, kite-flying has developed into a national pastime in Korea and Japan which received their culture from the mother-country.
note: Kite-flying is a national pastime in Korea, received from China; the kite as scapegoat for sins and misfortune is more developed there than in China.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: Since that time large kites have been prohibited in Owari.
note: Kite-flying is a national pastime received from China; traditions tell of men riding giant kites to spy or steal (Yui-no Shosetsu, Ishikawa Goyemon, Tametomo's son), after which large kites were banned in Owari and Edo.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: From China kites were diffused to all other nations of eastern Asia who experienced the influence of Chinese civilization—Korea, Japan, Annam, Camboja, Siam, Malaysia, inclusive of the Philippines and Borneo.
note: Kites reached Annam from China.

title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: Kites were introduced into India from China either through the Malays or Chinese immigrants or both. Kite-flying is a popular amusement in India during the spring. Matches are often made for considerable stakes.
note: Kites reached India from China via Malays or Chinese; kite-flying is a spring amusement with matches for large stakes, glass-coated strings to cut rivals, and respectable elderly men taking part.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: Al-Jāhiz, who died in A.D. 869, in his Book of Animals (Kitāb al-hayawān), speaks of "flags of the boys which were made of Chinese carton and paper; to these tails and wings were attached, little bells were tied to their fronts, and on breezy days they were released into the air from long and firm threads."
note: Al-Jahiz (9th century) describes boys' kites of Chinese paper with tails, wings and bells flown on long threads; Musailima, Muhammad's rival, is said to have used kites with musical bows at night to feign talking with angels.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: Kite-flying is well known to the Turks as a sport both for children and adults. The kite is called in Osmanli kartal ("eagle"), in Jagatai and Cumanian sar ("sparrow-hawk").
note: Kite-flying is a sport of Turkish children and adults; Ottoman kartal (eagle), Chagatay and Cuman sar (sparrow-hawk).

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: Francesco Lana (1670, p. 50) informs us that in his time kites were manipulated by the children of Italy. He calls them drago ("dragon"), while the Italians now designate them aquilone ("north wind"), cometa ("comet"), or cervo-volante ("flying-stag")
note: Italian children flew kites by 1670; names drago, aquilone, cometa and cervo-volante.

author: Laufer, Berthold
title: The prehistory of aviation. Field Museum of Natural History, Anthropological Series 18(1). Chicago
text: In the middle of the seventeenth century kites were commonly employed in England for the purpose of letting off fireworks.
note: English kites, introduced from the East, were used in the seventeenth century to let off fireworks (Bate's lozenge-shaped linen kite with a tail, 1634) and were a children's pastime by Strutt's time (1801).
link_note: No EA match; the EA New Englanders are not used.

title: Kite-fishing. In: Essays and Studies Presented to William Ridgeway, ed. E. C. Quiggin, pp. 583-608. Cambridge
text: In reading the Daily Mail of September 21, 1901, my eye was arrested by the following head-lines: 'Sea fishing by Kites. The remarkable Invention of an Enthusiastic Angler.'
note: An English angler flew box-kites from a long wire to carry baited lines out to sea on an off-shore breeze; Balfour treats it as a recent independent invention of a device long used in the Eastern Seas.
link_note: English kite fishing of 1901, kept apart from the British (1714-1815) eHRAF file.

author: Plischke, Hans

text: Der von den Fischern bei Singapore verwendete Drachen besteht aus Palmblättern. Auf der Malaiischen Halbinsel werden auch die Spieldrachen aus Palmblättern und nicht aus Papier verfertigt, allerdings mit dem Unterschied, daß die Spieldrachen kunstvoller und sorgfältiger gebaut werden.
note: Singapore fishermen use palm-leaf fishing kites, brought only recently by a fisherman from Java; on the Malay Peninsula play kites are also of palm leaf but more carefully made.

author: Plischke, Hans

text: Auf Java werden die für Sport und Spiel benutzten Drachen kunstvoll aus buntem Papier verfertigt, während die Fischdrachen Indonesiens und auch die von West-Java aus einem getrockneten Blatte hergestellt werden.
note: Fishermen of Tanara and the Thousand Islands fish from anchored praus with a rod-flown kite of an unstiffened fern leaf and a baited fibre noose; Javanese play kites are of coloured paper, called lajangan.

text: Im selben Gebiet, auf Andonare und an der Ostspitze von Flores, sah bereits in der ersten Hälfte des 19. Jahrhunderts der niederländische Seefahrer Reinwardt die Eingebornen mit Hilfe eines „vliegers“ d. h. mit Hilfe eines Drachens dem Fischfang nachgehen.
note: Reinwardt (1821) saw people of Adonara and east Flores fishing with kites and a hook; Jacobsen later saw, from a sailing boat off north Flores, a carefully made palm-leaf kite (a rectangle topped by a triangle) trailing a lure of lawalawa spider web.

note: Weber saw Talaud fishermen fly a kite of a dried leaf stiffened with two rods, the line on a wooden spool, trailing a hook with a small fish.

author: Plischke, Hans

text: Als kurz vor Ausbruch des Weltkrieges Dr. Burger auf Banda-nera weilte, konnte er beobachten, wie die Eingebornen dieser Insel Drachen steigen ließen, deren Schweife bis zum Meeresspiegel herabfielen.
note: Plischke gives Middleton's voyage of 1604-06 as the oldest record of kite fishing in the region (Anell places Middleton's picture on Ternate); on Banda kite fishing is recorded by Weber, at the 1880 Berlin fisheries exhibition, and by Burger on Banda Neira; two men fish from a boat with a kite of a long leaf or sewn leaf strips and a copper noose or spider-web lure; the method is named sakarawang after the spider.
link_note: The Banda records describe kite fishing on Banda Neira between 1880 and 1913, after the Dutch conquest of 1621 had largely replaced the population; linked to Banda Malay, the language of the islands since then, rather than to Banda, which is now spoken in the Kei Islands. The older picture from Middleton's voyage of 1604-06, which Plischke lists first, is from Ternate (Anell 1955: 35-36).

note: A rectangular fishing kite of sewn pandanus strips with a plant-fibre line (lolaki) and an 11 cm spider-web lure, used in the south-east monsoon (Müller-Wismar's specimen in Leipzig).

note: Admiralty Islanders fish with a pointed elliptical kite of banana leaf on a rod frame, its edges cut into small triangles and hung with leaf pennants, the 60-80 m line wound on a forked stick and tied to the canoe; the lure is said to be of caterpillar cocoons.

note: Siassi fishing kites (katap) are the smallest in Melanesia, about 13 cm, roughly triangular, of two taro leaves stiffened with leaf ribs, with a loose spider-web lure.
