note: Fishing kites are used on the Tami Islands; spider-web lures are known in the Huon Gulf.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf der Insel Dobu in der d’Entrecasteaux-Gruppe wird der Drachen aus drei oder vier Blättern, die je 30 cm lang und 7 bis 10 cm breit sind, zusammengesetzt.
note: Dobu fishing kites (daune) are elongated triangles of three or four sewn Morinda leaves on a stick frame with leaf tassels, flown on about 400 m of line with a 60-80 m tail; spiders are kept in bamboo to spin the web for the 12 cm lure.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Normanby-I., ebenda.
note: Fishing kite recorded for Normanby Island (after Murray).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Goodenough-I. Murray, Papua or British New Guinea, London 1912, S. 117—118.
note: Fishing kite recorded for Goodenough Island (after Murray); the language assignment (Bwaidoka) is approximate.
link_note: EA Bwaidoga (Goodenough Island) used as proxy.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Fergusson-I. Murray, Papua or British New Guinea, London 1912, S. 117—118.
note: Fishing kite recorded for Fergusson Island (after Murray).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf der Kitava-Insel der Trobriand-Gruppe hat der Köder die Form eines kleinen Tennisschlägers.
note: On Kitava the spider-web lure is wound on a small racquet-like frame, which also serves as the lure.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Eine abweichende Form hat der Fischdrachen von den Marshall Bennet-Inseln, von denen Seligmann ein Exemplar dem Pitt Rivers Museum zu Oxford überwies (Tafel 2, Fig. 5). Seine Gestalt ist oval.
note: An oval fishing kite of sewn palm-leaf strips with a long narrow tail, about 90 by 40 cm.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf Neuguinea läßt sich der Spieldrachen für die Motu-Motu im Elema-Distrikt nachweisen.
note: Play kites recorded for the Motu-Motu (Toaripi) of the Elema district.
link_note: Motu-Motu, Elema district (Plischke); Toaripi is the language of the Motumotu.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Ebensowenig ist er auf den Inseln der Torresstraße, wie überhaupt an der Südküste Neuguineas in Gebrauch.
note: The fishing kite is not used in the Torres Strait or on the south coast of New Guinea.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: In der Nähe des Kaps Laverdie an der Nordküste von Bougainville sah der Reisende Zöller, wie in der Nähe des Strandes Auslegerboote auf dem Meere lagen, „die sich den Scherz machten, in Form und Aussehen dem bekannten Spielzeug europäischer Kinder gleichende Drachen steigen zu lassen“.
note: Zöller saw outrigger canoes flying kites near Cape Laverdie, which Plischke takes for fishing kites; northern Solomons fishing kites are triangles up to 2 m long with three tails, trailing a tortoiseshell or pearl-shell trolling hook, the line tied to the canoe.
link_note: EA Kurtatchi (Tinputz-speaking north-east Bougainville).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Ebenso läßt sich diese Fischfangmethode für die Insel Buka belegen.
note: Kite-fishing recorded for Buka (after Parkinson); the line is tied to the canoe.
link_note: Plischke's Buka (after Parkinson) is not localised further; linked to Halia, the most widely spoken language of Buka Island, as a proxy.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Diese Annahme erhält erhöhte Berechtigung, wenn man berücksichtigt, daß im Gebiet der Insel Neugeorgien Ribbe den Fischdrachen beobachten konnte.
note: Ribbe observed the fishing kite in the New Georgia area, confirming Balfour's reading of a New Georgian drawing.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf Malaita wird der Drachen aus Streifen trockner Sago- oder Steinnußblätter in rechteckiger Form aneinandergenäht.
note: Malaita fishing kites (rau) are rectangles of sewn sago or ivory-nut leaf strips, about 80 by 30 cm, with three pointed tails and a thread bridle; the line is held in the teeth or hand and the oval spider-web loop can be reused about ten times.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Für die südlich von Malaita gelegene Insel Ulawa ist der Fischfang mit dem Drachen ebenfalls bezeugt.
note: Kite-fishing attested for Ulawa (after Coombe).
link_note: EA Ulawans.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf Santa Anna, südlich von San Christoval, haben sie die Gestalt eines Trapezes, auf dessen oberer breiterer Seite ein Dreieck aufgesetzt ist.
note: Santa Ana fishing kites are trapezoids topped by a triangle, of sewn palm-leaf strips, about 50 by 30 cm.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Dieser Drachen erinnert in seiner Form an einen mit ausgebreiteten Schwingen fliegenden Vogel.
note: Reef Islands fishing kites of sewn palm-leaf strips are shaped like a bird with spread wings; Coombe took one for a large bird over the sea until told it was a fishing kite.
link_note: Records do not say which of the Reef Islands. Linked to Äiwoo, the language of the eastern Reef Islands, although the people of the western Reef Islands and Taumako speak a Polynesian language, Vaeakau-Taumako (Barton and Dietrich 2009: 91).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf den Santa Cruz-Inseln soll der erste Fisch, den man gefangen hat, als Lockmittel bei weiteren Fängen benutzt werden
note: Fishing kites in the Santa Cruz group, said by Jennings to be of barkcloth on a bamboo frame and by Speiser to be of leaves; the first fish caught is used as a decoy and others are taken with a hand net.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Bereits auf den Banks-Inseln und den Neuen Hebriden fehlt sie. [...] Auf den Banks-Inseln und den Neuen Hebriden kennt man ihn nicht mehr, obwohl man dort das Steigenlassen von Drachen übt.
note: Banks Islanders fly play kites (rea) but have no fishing kite.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Neue Hebriden, Lepers-Insel, mala. S. mala bedeutet ein großer Vogel.
note: Play kites on Ambae are called mala, a big bird; the New Hebrides know only the play kite.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Neucaledonien kannte den Drachen nicht.
note: Kites were unknown in New Caledonia.
link_note: EA Ajie used as a New Caledonian proxy.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf Fidji war er ebenfalls unbekannt. Als dort eines Tages ein Missionar einen Drachen steigen ließ, erregte er das Staunen und die Freude der Eingebornen.
note: Kites were unknown in Fiji; a missionary's kite astonished the people, who called it manumanu, bird (after Seemann).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Ein Mann, der von der Insel Rotuma stammte und beim Steigenlassen des Drachens zugegen war, kannte den Drachen von seiner Heimatinsel. Mit den Angaben des Eingebornen von Rotuma stimmen die späteren Beobachtungen überein.
note: A Rotuman present when the missionary flew a kite in Fiji knew kites from his home island, confirmed by Gardiner's later account.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Die Australier kannten weder Spiel- noch Fischdrachen.
note: Aboriginal Australians knew neither play nor fishing kites; kites among Queensland children reflect recent Malay or European influence.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: während bei dem Vorkommen auf Sansibar auch an malaiische Beeinflussung gedacht werden darf.
note: Kites occur on Zanzibar (after Hildebrandt), perhaps through Malay influence.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Dasselbe gilt übrigens auch für den einzigen westafrikanischen Beleg, den ich für die Bekanntschaft des Negers mit dem Drachen auffinden konnte. Er stammt aus dem Jahre 1727.
note: A single West African record of kites, from 1727, which Plischke attributes to European influence.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Der Kulturbesitz der Palau-Insulaner kennt den Fischdrachen nicht, obgleich er auf den Inseln der Nachbarschaft bekannt ist. Wohl aber sind dort Feste, bei denen man Drachen steigen läßt, von großer Bedeutung.
note: Palauans have no fishing kite (Krämer's report is doubted) but kite-flying festivals are of great importance; the kite is named kadscham after the bird kadschman said to have brought it to Palau (after Kubary).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Nur auf der südlich von Palau gelegenen Insel Tobi läßt man den Fischdrachen vom Strand aus steigen.
note: On Tobi the fishing kite is flown from the reef edge on a long rod held by a boy (Krämer's photographs), the only shore-flown fishing kite recorded.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Der Drachen von Songosor (Tafel 1, Fig. 5), der sich unter den Beständen des Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig befindet, stimmt im Bau mit den Drachen von den Zentralkarolinen überein
note: Sonsorol fishing kites (sauri gesseik) are made of a breadfruit leaf stiffened with ribs, used to catch the garfish magi.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Der Fischdrache kommt weder auf Jap, noch auf Mogmog vor
note: Müller-Wismar states the fishing kite occurs neither on Yap nor Mogmog, against Krämer; Yap is among the islands where bird-shaped kites are flown at religious festivals.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Der Fischdrache kommt weder auf Jap, noch auf Mogmog vor
note: The fishing kite does not occur on Mogmog (after Müller-Wismar).
link_note: EA Ulithians.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Sicher belegt ist der Fischdrachen für die Inseln Oleai und Lamutrik
note: Fishing kites are securely recorded for Woleai and Lamotrek: a deeply lobed breadfruit leaf up to 75 by 52 cm, stiffened with ribs, the bait a ball of fish sinew.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Weiterhin erwähnt Krämer, daß die Bewohner der Insel Truk den Fischdrachen besitzen.
note: Krämer reports the fishing kite on Truk.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf vielen Inseln Mikronesiens, so auf den Marianen, den Palau-Inseln, auf Jap, Kusae und Nauru, auf den Marshall- und Gilbert-Inseln läßt man Drachen nicht zum Fischfang, wohl aber bei religiösen Festen steigen.
note: In the Marianas kites are flown at religious festivals, not for fishing; the kite game on Saipan is called papalote (after Fritz).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf vielen Inseln Mikronesiens, so auf den Marianen, den Palau-Inseln, auf Jap, Kusae und Nauru, auf den Marshall- und Gilbert-Inseln läßt man Drachen nicht zum Fischfang, wohl aber bei religiösen Festen steigen.
note: On Kosrae kites are flown at religious festivals; the kite game is kuk palpal (after Sarfert).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf vielen Inseln Mikronesiens, so auf den Marianen, den Palau-Inseln, auf Jap, Kusae und Nauru, auf den Marshall- und Gilbert-Inseln läßt man Drachen nicht zum Fischfang, wohl aber bei religiösen Festen steigen.
note: On Nauru kites (edauidaue) are flown at religious festivals (after Hambruch).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf vielen Inseln Mikronesiens, so auf den Marianen, den Palau-Inseln, auf Jap, Kusae und Nauru, auf den Marshall- und Gilbert-Inseln läßt man Drachen nicht zum Fischfang, wohl aber bei religiösen Festen steigen.
note: In the Marshalls kites are flown at religious festivals; lim-ak-ak means folded like a frigate bird (after Erdland).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Auf vielen Inseln Mikronesiens, so auf den Marianen, den Palau-Inseln, auf Jap, Kusae und Nauru, auf den Marshall- und Gilbert-Inseln läßt man Drachen nicht zum Fischfang, wohl aber bei religiösen Festen steigen.
note: Gilbert Islanders fly kites at religious festivals, with names for kinds of kite (Bingham's dictionary), though Krämer saw none there.
link_note: Gilbertese; EA Makin (northern Gilberts) used as the Ethnographic Atlas proxy.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: manu aute. S. aute ist die aus der Rinde von Brousonetia papyrifera hergestellte Tapa, aus der man auf Neuseeland früher den ganzen Körper eines Drachens verfertigte. Heute nimmt man dazu meist Blätter; nur der Kopf des Drachens besteht noch aus aute.
term: manu; manu aute; manu waka-tuku-tuku; pakau; kahu
note: Maori kite names manu (bird), manu aute, manu waka-tuku-tuku, pakau (wing) and kahu (hawk); kites were once wholly of aute barkcloth, later of leaves with only the head of aute. Plischke says Polynesian kite-flying generally carried religious meaning.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: ua-moa. S. Ein eiförmiger, aus Blättern verfertigter Drachen. Auf Mangaia. [...] perue. S. In Gestalt eines mit ausgebreiteten Schwingen fliegenden Vogels. [...] taiaro. S. In Gestalt einer Keule.
note: Mangaian kites: ua-moa, egg-shaped of leaves; perue, a bird with spread wings; taiaro, club-shaped; manu, bird, for all kinds (after Gill).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Aber dann muß darauf hingewiesen werden, daß der Drachen sich für die Gesellschafts-Inseln zu einer Zeit nachweisen läßt, wo europäische Beeinflussung unbedingt ausgeschlossen ist
note: Tahitian kite words pauma and uo; Boenechea's diary of 1772-76 shows kites in Tahiti before any European influence, against Kubary's view that Europeans introduced them.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: pauma. S. Nach Tregear, A Paumotuan Dictionary.
note: Tuamotuan kite word pauma.
link_note: EA Raroians (Tuamotus).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: manu uru, S. Nach Churchill, Easter Island.
note: Easter Island kite word manu uru.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: lupe. S. Nach Culin, Hawaiian Games. American Anthropologist. N. S. Bd. 1. S. 224. Dort auch die Benennungen für die einzelnen Formen, die man den Drachen auf Hawaii gibt.
note: Hawaiian kites (lupe) come in named forms and use a thread bridle (after Culin).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Markesas-Inseln: Nach brieflicher Mitteilung, die ich Herrn Prof. Dr. von den Steinen verdanke.
note: Kites known in the Marquesas (letter from von den Steinen).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Samoa: Drachen unbekannt.
note: Kites unknown in Samoa (after Brown).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Tonga-Inseln: Drachen unbekannt. W. Mariner, An Account of the Natives of the Tonga-Islands, London 1817. 2 Bände, erwähnt den Drachen nicht.
note: Kites unknown in Tonga, inferred from Mariner's silence.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Als die Erfinder des Flächendrachens müssen zweifellos die Chinesen betrachtet werden.
note: Plischke credits the Chinese with inventing the plane kite, which spread east through Polynesia and west to Europe in the 16th century with the Portuguese.
link_note: EA Kiangsu used as a Han Chinese proxy.

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Von China ist der Drachen nach Japan gekommen.
note: The kite reached Japan from China (after W. Müller).

author: Plischke, Hans
title: Der Fischdrachen. Veröffentlichungen des Städtischen Museums für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig, Heft 6. Leipzig
text: Für Europa läßt sich allerdings ein Zeugnis bringen. Die Daily Mail vom 21. September 1901 veröffentlicht unter dem Titel „Sea-Fishing by Kites […]“ ein Bild, auf dem Engländer einen Kastendrachen in die Luft steigen lassen, dessen Schwanzende zur Oberfläche des Wassers reicht und am Ende einen Köder trägt.
note: Plischke cites the Daily Mail of 21 September 1901 for Englishmen fishing with a box kite whose tail carries bait at the water's surface; he leaves open whether this was an independent invention and suggests English sport anglers may have taken up the method from Indonesia and Melanesia.
link_note: English kite fishing of 1901, kept apart from the British (1714-1815) eHRAF file.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The inhabitants of the island of Rathman in the Pelew group are said to hold kite-flying festivals at irregular intervals.
note: Kite-flying festivals at irregular intervals honour the gannet, a sacred bird after which the kites are named; from time to time the god orders a big long-tailed kite to be made and the whole population flies it from treeless heights (Kubary, via Frazer).

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: KITE MADE, OF PLAITED LEAVES, FROM YAP, CAROLINE ISLANDS (214 x 114 CM.).
note: Figure of a plaited-leaf kite from Yap, 214 by 114 cm (after Müller).

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The Gilbert Islanders and those of the Kingsmill group are also said to make fine kites of sewed pandanus leaves.
note: Gilbert Islanders make fine kites of sewn pandanus leaves.
link_note: Gilbertese; EA Makin (northern Gilberts) used as the Ethnographic Atlas proxy.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: DIAGRAMMATIC SKETCH OF KITE, FROM NAURU, GILBERT ISLANDS (BREADTH OVER 2 METRES).
note: Figure of a Nauru kite over 2 m wide (after Hambruch).

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: Gill tells us that the Mangaian kites were generally five feet in length and covered with native tapa, or bark cloth, on which devices appropriate to the tribe were stained as a kind of heraldry.
note: Mangaian kites of tapa about five feet long bore tribal devices, their tails up to twenty fathoms with feathers and ti-leaf bunches numbered after constellations, in bird, egg and club shapes (manu, bird); parties of ten or more grey-bearded fliers competed for height with songs, each kite named, the first kite of a contest dedicated to Rongo, god of the dead and of kite-flying, to whom the art's origin is attributed; kite-songs (the Twin Kites, adapted c. 1770; Tenio's Fete, c. 1814) were performed at commemoration festivals for dead chiefs, and in one Rongo beats Tane at kite-flying with the longer string.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: A famous kite in Rarotonga, which is said to have been about twelve feet long by six feet wide, was known as Rua-kapanga, the name of the sacred bird of Tane.
note: A famous kite about twelve by six feet was named Rua-kapanga after Tane's sacred bird, and a lament for that bird may be a kite-song; kite-songs opened kite-flying competitions; the sport is said to be very old; in the Rata tale the priest Nganaoa joins Rata's canoe as a kite-flyer and destroys sea monsters, which Chadwick reads as a demon-quelling kite (the Aitutaki variant, which she compares, does not mention the kite).
link_note: No EA match; Mangaian EA codes are not transferred to Rarotonga.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The ancient kites of Tahiti were sometimes of immense size and required three or four men to hold them as they soared.
note: Ancient Tahitian kites, some needing three or four men, were shaped as men, turtles and frigate birds and carried sacred feathers; flown by men and boys (after Henry). Chadwick infers kites in war from Ellis's account of Tane and Ra advancing before warriors waving comet-like tails, reads the legend of Honoura rising above Mount Tahuareva as a kite, and links the royal language (the king 'flying', mahuta) to kite symbolism; the legend does not name a kite.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The modern Hawaiian kites are six-sided in shape.
note: Modern Hawaiian kites are six-sided, about six by four and a half feet, of kapa, with very long cords and fifteen-fathom tails, held by two men; chants of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries speak of the kites of the kapu chiefs and of chiefs as kites, the Creation Chant of kites striking and adhering together, the Kawelo legend of entangling a rival's kite; Westervelt's Maui tales tell of a kite larger than a house raised with a kite-song to the winds, a bird-kite of ti-leaves and feathers carrying Maui, the kite as a sign of dry weather and as a tow for his canoe. Chadwick adds military reconnaissance.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: It was said to be a recognized sign of peace when kites were seen flying near a Maori village.
note: The Maori kite (kahu, hawk) imitated the bird; kites near a village signalled peace; kites were once used for divination and are said still to serve as a weather gauge; large kites, some five yards across, were named after an owner's ancestor; a kite with a firebrand was flown at night as a fiery demon; kite-songs (Shortland, Best) opened competitions; the sport is said to be very old; Tawhaki ascends to heaven as or by a kite, Whakatau flies kites in a match and from under water, Maui is an adept.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: We shall see presently that Tawhaki is represented in Moriori chants as singing a karakia as he mounts to heaven in the form of a kite.
note: Moriori 'Tawhaki' poems are recited as charms against bad weather and at sea; Chadwick reads the third, spoken by the hero battling the winds and asking to be held by hand, as Tawhaki in kite form, though the chant does not name a kite.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491

note: Chadwick reads the Paumotu version of the Onokura (Honoura) legend, in which the hero rises into the sky, as a kite rising to a kite-song; the legend does not name a kite.
link_note: EA Raroians (Tuamotus).

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The ritual character of kite-flying is perhaps shown most clearly in the custom of accompanying the ascent of a kite by a chant or karakia called a kite-song. [...] Codrington records another from Lepers Island in Melanesia (see p. 470 below), where kite-fishing is practised.
note: Codrington records a Lepers Island kite-song calling the wind to carry the kite far away; Chadwick says kite fishing is practised there, against Plischke and Anell, who report only play kites in the New Hebrides. Ritual coded from the kite-song alone; excluded in the strict ritual sensitivity.

title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491

note: Kite-flying is much in vogue and pursued by adults; Skeat and Blagden record a Malay kite-song which they think refers to kite fishing; fishing kites occur from Singapore eastwards. Ritual coded from the kite-song alone, which Chadwick takes from Skeat and Blagden; excluded in the strict ritual sensitivity.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: In Java it is almost a national passion, and kite-flying contests are carried on with an elaborate betting system comparable to our own horse-racing.
note: Kite-flying is a near-national passion of adults, with contests and elaborate betting; Javanese kite-fighting fouls the opponent's kite; some kites carry a musical bow; fishing kites are flown from a rod fixed through a hole in a canoe plank.

text: GIANT KITE ON THE ISLAND OF BALI. RELIGIOUS DANCES ARE IN PROGRESS BEFORE A HINDU TEMPLE.
note: Kite-flying is pursued by adults; a plate shows a giant kite during religious dances before a temple. Ritual coded from the plate caption alone; excluded in the strict ritual sensitivity.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: At Kyoto, Tokio, and Nagasaki great kite-flying contests are held on certain days of the year.
note: Great contests are held on set days at Kyoto, Tokyo and Nagasaki, where fighters cut rivals' strings with glass-coated lines; kites in bird, fish and demon shapes, some with musical bows; Nagasaki children fly the oni-dako (devil kite) and kites bear the demon-queller Shoki; in Suruga boys fly kites on kite's day, losing one is very unlucky and search parties follow it up to twenty miles, and girls never have kites; traditions tell of man-lifting kites for reconnaissance, Ishikawa Goemon's night flight and Ui Shosetsu.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: They are flown chiefly by men and boys; and all classes, from the king downwards, fly kites.
note: Korean kites in fantastic shapes and striped colours include wind harps; flown by all classes, they serve as demon-quellers and scapegoats, a wish that the year's misfortunes be carried away written on them on the fourteenth of the first month; legends credit a general with inventing the kite to raise a lantern as a new star and another with bridging a stream by kite.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: Kite-flying is widely practised in China by both old and young, and here its religious associations are well established.
note: Peasants keep kites over their houses to frighten evil spirits and use them as scapegoats; on the ninth of the ninth month (kite's day in Fujian) thirty to forty thousand people fly kites in bird, human, fish, tiger and snake shapes on the hills, for health and against ill-luck; wind harps are common; Liu Ngan's account of Mih Tih's wooden kite is the earliest record, and Han Sin is said to have used kites for signalling and measuring; Chadwick derives the kite from early China.
link_note: EA Kiangsu used as a Han Chinese proxy.

note: When the eldest son reaches seven, his father makes a straw kite and lets it fly away carrying off all evil, in a ceremony called driving away the devil (Andree, via Frazer).

note: Kite-flying is pursued by adults throughout Indonesia; sailors of the old East Indiamen reported that kites seen from ships off the Malaysian islands were withdrawn when strangers approached, as if too sacred to be watched, and spoke of kites sent up as a religious rite (Woglom); Chadwick applies this to Polynesia.

author: Chadwick, Nora K.
title: The kite: a study in Polynesian tradition. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 61: 455-491
text: The kite is a religious symbol and represents the soul. It is a demon-queller.
note: Chadwick concludes that Polynesian kite-flying was a cult in which each person's kite, a bird symbol, was his external soul and a demon-queller, tied to Rongo, Tane and Rehua and to Tawhaki's chiefly line; tradition and practice refer only to men; tohungas also used kites in weather lore and navigation; the art is old in Polynesia but was brought from eastern or central Asia, and declined after about AD 750.

text: The kite is not found on the Polynesian outliers, e.g. on Ontong Java
note: The fishing kite is absent from the Polynesian outliers of the Solomons, for example Ontong Java.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: The kite, batoa, is made of leaf of pandanus, sewn together, and supported by ribs of the leaf.
note: On Petats Chinnery describes a triangular kite (batoa) of sewn pandanus leaf braced with split cane, trailing a spider web that swells when wet; Blackwood's kite (vavatoa) of five leaf strips is lyre-shaped, its prolonged outer strips perhaps meant to make it bird-like.
link_note: Blackwood's kite-fishing passages name Petats informants and dialect terms; moved from the Tinputz file.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala

note: Anell reads Zöller's report from the Buka Passage region as kite-flying with no mention of fishing; Plischke had taken Zöller's canoe kites off Cape Laverdie for fishing kites.
link_note: EA Kurtatchi (Tinputz-speaking north-east Bougainville).

author: Anell, Bengt

note: A fishing kite (dala) of ivory-palm leaf strips on Santa Isabel.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: A peculiar type of kite, belama, the frigate-bird, occurs on Roviana.
note: Kites are used both for fishing and as toys on Roviana; the belama kite reproduces the conventional frigate-bird figure and is said to catch sea-snakes, though Anell thinks garfish are the game; Guppy's bird-shaped kites may be this type.

author: Anell, Bengt

note: Kites are used both for fishing and as toys in the Florida Islands.

author: Anell, Bengt

note: The Malaita fishing kite is rectangular with two cross-ribs, a straight top edge and a three-lobed lower edge formed by the prolonged outer and middle strips, which Anell takes as meant to give a bird-like look.

author: Anell, Bengt

note: The Guadalcanal fishing kite is rectangular with a prolonged midrib and outer strips, double cross-ribs and outer ribs from the strips' midveins.

author: Anell, Bengt

text: Kite fishing has also occurred on the Santa Cruz Islands.
note: Santa Cruz fishing kites are of leaf strips (Coombe: also bark) with the middle strips prolonged upwards, a midrib, two cross-ribs and two streamers; reports of hooks or gorges confuse kite fishing with the flying-fish method.

note: Play kites in the Elema district, the only play-kite record for northern and western Melanesia.
link_note: Anell cites Holmes (1908: 282), who describes kites (ori) among the Toaripi and the Morea-ipi; the Morea-ipi words in his paper show the sound changes of Orokolo, and Holmes lived at Orokolo from 1897. Linked to Orokolo; Plischke's Motumotu record is coded Toaripi.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: Kite-fishing does not occur in Polynesia. Kite-flying as a pastime, on the other hand, is common, and there are frequent allusions to this in the folklore
note: Polynesia has play kites, common in folklore, but no fishing kite. Anell rejects Balfour's and Plischke's view that the kite was kept out of fishing as a cult object, and thinks Polynesians and eastern Micronesians reached their islands with the flying kite before the fishing kite was invented.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: It is regarded as an established fact that in the Singapore area the fishing-kite was introduced by immigrants from Java.
note: The Malacca Strait fishing kite is a single unstiffened leaf, usually Polypodium, with a noose round a small bait fish, the line run through a ring at the top of a rod; it came to Singapore with Javanese immigrants.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: As regards the Javanese kite, it is said to have been introduced from the southern Celebes by the Bugineses, which may be possible, although kite-fishing is nowhere mentioned from this region
note: North-west Java and the Thousand Islands have the single-leaf, skeleton-less fishing kite with a baited noose and a ringed rod; it is said to have come from South Celebes with the Bugis, which Anell allows though kite fishing is not reported there.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: The type of fishing kite that is known from the Malacca Sound, from the north-western coast of Java, Bawean and the Thousand Islands, is of the most primitive kind.
note: Bawean has the single-leaf fishing kite with noose and rod, as in west Java.

locality: east Flores; Larantuka Strait; Tanah Boleng and Wureh, Adonara; Solor
author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: From the east coast of Flores, for the rest, kite-fishing is mentioned even by Reinwardt, who observed with surprise the natives fishing with "vlieger".
note: On Flores the fishing kite is of several leaves with a backbone, two cross-ribs and a tail, baited with cobweb (lawalawa); at Tanah Boleng on Adonara it is a single leaf, at Wureh of leaf strips; at Larantuka Strait, also on the Solor side, it is of sewn pandanus strips with a backbone nearly 2.5 m long and a tangle of silk threads as lure (after Jacobsen, Reinwardt and Vatter).
link_note: EA Ili-Mandiri (Lamaholot).

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: The kite found on Pura is considerably bigger than the one from Larantuka Sound, but not, on the other hand, so well made. [...] The material consists of strips of pandanus leaf, not sewn together [...] Cobweb is used as bait.
note: The Pura fishing kite is a rectangle of unsewn pandanus strips pinned with palm-leaf ribs, 110 by 55 cm, on a backbone nearly 2 m long, with a cobweb lure (after Vatter).

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: From Ternate there is an early picture of kite-fishing with rod reproduced by Middleton.
note: Middleton's early picture shows kite fishing with a rod on Ternate; Weber reports a bait line ending in a copper-wire noose and the line run through a ring at the top of the rod, as on Java.

author: Anell, Bengt
title: The fishing kite. Ch. IV in Contribution to the History of Fishing in the Southern Seas, pp. 29-41. Studia Ethnographica Upsaliensia 9. Uppsala
text: This is 64 x 18 cm; it is used with a rod, and the bait-line ends in a noose of brass wire
note: Banda fishing kites include Burger's rod-flown kite with a brass-wire noose, a single lance-shaped leaf of rio from Ceram with a spider-web lure, and Plischke's broad oval frame covered with sewn leaf strips. Balfour and Plischke place the origin of kite fishing in Banda, where all variants meet; Anell finds Banda or north-western Melanesia equally possible.
link_note: The Banda records describe kite fishing on Banda Neira between 1880 and 1913, after the Dutch conquest of 1621 had largely replaced the population; linked to Banda Malay, the language of the islands since then, rather than to Banda, which is now spoken in the Kei Islands. The older picture from Middleton's voyage of 1604-06, which Plischke lists first, is from Ternate (Anell 1955: 35-36).

note: A rectangular Babar fishing kite of leaf strips with a vertical rib and four pairs of cross-ribs, 60 by 25 cm, on a liana line ending in a spider-web wad.

note: Ambon kite fishing uses as lure the beaten-out nest of a giant poisonous spider from Gunung Api.

note: The Karakelang fishing kite is a single leaf on two crossed sticks, with a hook on the bait line and the hand line on a spool (after Weber); Anell thinks the Carolinian fishing kite came from here.
